solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Page 1's unusual marine animal

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so these letters are set in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
the numeral 1 is the Roman I, and with its 's it gives IS

explanation.surface: A reference book's first page describes some strange creature of the deep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Page 1's' looks like a page reference; mixed up by 'unusual', PAGE plus I'S gives the creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea pig is a deep-sea cucumber, a real ocean creature, so it is a marine animal.

clue.text: Reserve it, or I'll have to panic (filling nappy)

indicators.note: the other pieces fill the nappy word, so they go inside it

parts.note: terry is the towelling cloth of old-fashioned British nappies, and a nappy can be called a terry
taken as written
taken as written
I'll is I will, giving the letter I as the one who will have to panic
alarm is a synonym of panic

explanation.surface: A parent warns that unless someone keeps it in reserve, nappy-changing will cause panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'filling' signals the insertion. Terry towelling was the cloth of traditional British washable nappies, so a nappy can be called a terry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Territorial Army was Britain's volunteer military reserve, so the name means a reserve force.

clue.text: Canonised person with a novel family tree

parts.note: a canonised person is a saint, abbreviated ST
Emma is a novel by Jane Austen

explanation.surface: A saint appears with a novel that traces a family's ancestry.
explanation.definitionFit: A stemma is a pedigree or diagram of descent, the scholarly word for a genealogical chart.

clue.text: What's unusually served out hot from counters? …

definitions.text: What's unusually served out hot from counters? …

indicators.note: used unusually, these letters fall into an odd new arrangement

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about some drink poured hot at bars, leading into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusually' rearranges HOT FROM COUNTERS. The whole clue also describes the American whiskey liqueur served across bar counters, linked by the dots to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Southern Comfort is a fruit-flavoured whiskey liqueur poured by bar staff, matching the picture of drinks served.

clue.text: … eco-party's plan to recycle what's served out in bars

parts.note: the Green Party is the eco-party
a chart is a plan or map
to reuse is to recycle

explanation.surface: An environmental party's scheme for recycling the drinks poured in pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots join it to the previous clue: both answers are liqueurs.
explanation.definitionFit: Green Chartreuse is a French herbal liqueur, a drink bar staff pour for customers.

clue.text: By church, house a festive riot of students in depravity

indicators.note: the pieces are placed in the word for depravity, inside it

parts.note: vice is depravity
a rag is a British students' charity festival full of pranks

explanation.surface: Next to the church, a wild student party breaks out amid depravity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' signals the insertion. Rag week is a British university festival of charity stunts, hence a festive riot of students.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicarage is the residence of a vicar, typically standing beside the parish church.

clue.text: Scroll halfway down, finding one's special friends in pursuit of sex (a deficiency for writer)

indicators.note: only the first half of the word scroll is kept, as if read halfway down

parts.note: one is the Roman I, its 's read as 'is'

indicators.note: the pieces sit in the word for sexual pursuit

parts.note: venery is an archaic word for the pursuit of sexual pleasure
pals are friends

explanation.surface: Reading a scroll, someone finds their friends chasing sex, a sorry lapse for a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'halfway down' keeps the first three of six letters; 'in' signals the insertion. Venery is an archaic word, and the definition is a cryptic way of naming a writer's ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrivener's palsy is an old name for writer's cramp, a disability affecting those who write by hand.

clue.text: Badly behaved child keeping as quiet as a military officer!

indicators.note: the child's word keeps the pieces held inside it

parts.note: a brat is a badly behaved child
taken as written
SH is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: A naughty child is told to stay as silent as a soldier on parade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' signals the insertion; the second 'as' merely links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass hat is informal British slang for a high-ranking officer, from the gold braid on the cap.

clue.text: One votes finally to swap for printing plate

indicators.note: the final pair of letters swap places

parts.note: an elector is one who votes

explanation.surface: A voter is told to switch at the last minute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally to swap' exchanges the last two letters, OR, of ELECTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: An electro is short for an electrotype, a copper-faced plate used in letterpress work.

clue.text: In retrospect, this isn't one telling the truth about AA vehicle!

indicators.note: looking back means the letters are read in reverse

parts.words: this isn't one telling the truth about AA
parts.note: a liar about the AA might claim the rival RAC: an RAC LIAR

explanation.surface: Someone untruthful about the Automobile Association and its breakdown vans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In retrospect' reverses RAC LIAR. The AA and the RAC are Britain's rival motoring breakdown organisations.
explanation.definitionFit: A railcar is a self-propelled railway carriage, a kind of passenger vehicle.

clue.text: Numbers — no application from them puts America to trouble

indicators.note: troubled letters are stirred up into a new order

explanation.surface: A sum with no practical use troubles the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: Pure mathematics studies numbers and structures for their own sake, without any practical use in mind.

clue.text: Spill tea on belly, something water-proof

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another comes after it

parts.note: the gut is the belly
a spill is a thin taper for lighting fires
cha is slang for tea

explanation.surface: Someone spills their tea on their stomach and needs something waterproof.
explanation.definitionFit: Gutta-percha is a latex used to insulate underwater cables because water does not pass through it.

clue.text: Old character living in Market Harborough

indicators.note: the letters live inside the town's name

explanation.surface: An elderly eccentric resides in a Leicestershire market town.
explanation.walkthrough: Market Harborough is a town in Leicestershire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Eth is a letter of the Old English alphabet, so an old written character.

clue.text: Lay hands on back…lowering around hip…down here…snip!

indicators.note: the word is turned back to front

parts.note: to grab is to lay hands on

indicators.note: the word for lowering goes around the other piece

parts.note: abasement is a lowering
in means fashionable, hip

explanation.surface: A massage-style sequence of instructions: hands on the back, down round the hip, then a snip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses and 'around' contains. The dotted definition pairs a basement's position with a snip, British slang for a bargain.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargain basement is a downstairs store area of cut-price goods, where cheap finds are sold.

clue.text: Retriever raised right (not wrong) bonnet

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the word reads upwards

parts.note: a Labrador retriever is a lab
moral means right as opposed to wrong

explanation.surface: A dog lifts up a hat that is correct, not mistaken.
explanation.definitionFit: A Balmoral is a flat Scottish woollen cap, a type of Highland bonnet.

clue.text: Without legal proof declaring this person cooks quite a lot up on Government

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word reads upwards

parts.words: this person cooks quite a lot
parts.note: Nigella Lawson is a famous TV cook
G abbreviates government, placed on, after, the other piece

explanation.surface: Someone claims, unproven, that a person cooks a great deal at the government's expense.
explanation.walkthrough: Nigella Lawson is a well-known British TV chef; her name read upwards gives ALLEGIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Alleging means asserting something without having proved it, as in a legal claim.

clue.text: Open country guide not going as far as Germany

indicators.note: the word stops before reaching the letter for Germany

parts.note: to lead is to guide
D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: A tour guide whose trip stops short of Germany in the countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: A lea is a poetic word for a meadow or open grassland.

clue.text: Revolutionary backing "wrong" Christmas broadcaster

indicators.note: backing means these words are read backwards

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law
Noel is Christmas
Sky is a British satellite broadcaster

explanation.surface: A rebel supports a so-called wrong Christmas TV station.
explanation.definitionFit: Trotsky was a leader of the Russian Revolution of 1917, a famous revolutionary.

clue.text: Part characterised by Bronson, gunslinger in fine form

indicators.note: only a part of these words is taken, the stretch inside them

explanation.surface: A film role played by Charles Bronson as a gunfighter on top form.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Bronson was an American actor known for westerns.
explanation.definitionFit: On song is British idiom for performing at one's best, like a singer in good voice.

clue.text: I support telescope and, looking up, see 17 ascending

definitions.text: I support telescope and, looking up, see 17 ascending

parts.words: I support telescope and, looking up, see 17 ascending
parts.note: the instrument rests its sighting tube on Y-shaped supports, and its letters read upwards give a word for flat plus the Y that ends 17

explanation.surface: An instrument stand speaks, describing looking up the column to see the revolutionary.
explanation.walkthrough: The Y is shared with the last letter of 17 (TROTSKY); reading upwards gives LEVEL then Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A Y-level is a surveyor's levelling instrument whose telescope sits in Y-shaped rests.

clue.text: Nobody called the manor about lavish former province

parts.note: O is nought, nobody
rang means phoned, called

indicators.note: the manor's word goes about the other piece

parts.note: an estate is a manor
free means generous, lavish

explanation.surface: No one telephoned the lord's house about some extravagant old region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' has the manor's word going round the lavish one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Orange Free State was a Boer republic, later a province of South Africa until 1994.

clue.text: Social worker's money purloined by a recluse

indicators.note: the money is taken by, held within, the recluse's word

parts.note: a loner is a recluse

explanation.surface: A hermit steals a social worker's cash.
explanation.definitionFit: An almoner was a hospital social worker in Britain, originally one who distributed alms.

clue.text: Get very mature, synthetic essence

indicators.note: something synthetic is artificially made up, so these letters are reconstituted

explanation.surface: An instruction to age something with an artificial essence.
explanation.definitionFit: To senesce is to grow old, a verb for biological ageing.
